# Abstract

# Introduction

Fish populations supply the world’s largest harvest of wild food, supporting livelihoods and nourishing billions of people [@barron2022]. This reliance, together with a history of overexploitation and stock collapses, has motivated decades of monitoring and applied population ecology to inform sustainable fishing practices [@hilborn2020]. Detailed demographic data have proven useful for this task by providing information on the strength of cohorts as they age and the impact of fishing [@hjort1914; @maunder2013]. Fisheries agencies therefore routinely collect age-structured biological and fisheries data for use in stock assessment models.

At their core, age-structured stock assessment models share the demographic logic of Leslie matrix models [@leslie1945], a staple in population ecology, while explicitly accounting for fishing removals [@beverton1957]. They link demographic processes to observations to estimate population trends and project responses to alternative fishing scenarios [@maunder2013]. Early approaches treated catch-at-age observations as exact [@fry1949; @gulland1965], while subsequent statistical frameworks accommodate observation errors [@fournier1982] and, in state-space formulations, process variation [@gudmundsson1994; @schnute1994]. These approaches underpin software frameworks such as ADAPT for calibrated virtual population analysis [@gavaris1988], Stock Synthesis for integrated statistical catch-at-age [@methot2013], and SAM for state-space assessments [@nielsen2014].

Applying and adapting these models requires users to navigate specialized data formats, model specifications, and diagnostic procedures [@punt2020]. For biologists and ecologists familiar with GLMs and GLMMs in R, learning these conventions may present a barrier to exploring alternative biological hypotheses. An interface built around familiar data structures and model formulas could make it easier to express assumptions about recruitment, mortality, selectivity, and catchability, and to examine their consequences.




*Previous draft*


Age-structured stock assessment models connect these observations through recruitment and the survival of cohorts over time. They share this demographic logic with age-structured population models used elsewhere in ecology [@leslie1945], while fisheries models explicitly account for removals through fishing [@beverton1957]. Combining catches, survey indices and biological observations allows analysts to estimate population trajectories and project their responses to specified fishing scenarios [@maunder2013]. Those inferences depend on assumptions about both population processes and observations. For example, fewer older fish in a survey may reflect changes in survival, the strength of earlier cohorts or the fraction of fish available to the survey. Explicitly representing population processes and observation error is therefore central to interpreting population time series [@devalpine2002].

Several assessment frameworks support these analyses. ADAPT calibrates virtual population analysis (VPA) against abundance indices to reconstruct historical numbers at age [@gavaris1988]. Stock Synthesis integrates multiple data sources within a statistical age-structured framework [@methot2013]. The a4a initiative explicitly sought to broaden access to stock assessment through familiar R formulas for recruitment, fishing mortality and catchability [@jardim2015]. SAM represents stochastic variation in abundance and fishing mortality [@nielsen2014], while WHAM supports statistical catch-at-age and state-space configurations with environmental covariates and processes that vary across ages and years [@stock2021]. Together, these frameworks provide substantial flexibility for investigating alternative population dynamics.

Computational tools have expanded the possibilities further. Template Model Builder (TMB) provides automatic differentiation and Laplace approximation for fitting models with latent processes [@kristensen2016], and RTMB makes this machinery available to models written in R [@kristensen2026]. Translating an ecological question into a fitted model nevertheless involves choosing population and observation relationships, specifying their variation and checking whether the data support the resulting estimates. For biologists familiar with R and regression formulas, including users of mixed-model packages such as glmmTMB [@brooks2017], an accessible interface can help connect those choices to their biological consequences. This motivates tools that make assumptions straightforward to specify, inspect and compare within a consistent analysis workflow.

Here we introduce the tiny assessment model, `tinyAM`, an R package designed to support that workflow. It combines tidy input tables [@wickham2014] with component settings and formulas for recruitment, cohort survival, fishing and natural mortality, survey catchability and observation error. Users can change individual assumptions and examine their consequences through shared tools for numerical checks, uncertainty summaries, residual diagnostics, simulation and forecasting. Printed summaries, model diagrams and interactive dashboards help users inspect the specification and results. “Tiny” refers to a compact modelling vocabulary in which complexity comes from combining understandable components. We demonstrate the approach by comparing fixed and time-varying natural mortality in Northern cod, checking numerical agreement with matched SAM specifications and translating curated assessments across the North Atlantic and North Pacific. These examples examine the consequences of alternative assumptions and the framework’s numerical agreement and applicability in specific settings.

## Abstract

WHAM spans statistical catch-at-age and state-space models and supports comparisons among them [@stock2021]. SAM and Stock Synthesis are established assessment frameworks [@nielsen2014; @methot2013].
- State tinyAM’s design goal. ### Northern cod worked example

**Biological question.** Does allowing natural mortality to vary over time improve predictions of Northern cod survey observations at age and change the inferred history of spawning-stock biomass (SSB)? The [2025 Northern cod assessment](https://publications.gc.ca/collections/collection_2026/mpo-dfo/fs70-5/Fs70-5-2026-026-eng.pdf) motivates the question through its analysis of natural mortality and prey availability. The worked example uses the packaged catch and survey observations to evaluate the more specific assumption about variation in mortality.

**Specify two alternatives.** Start with the NCAM-like fit in [the case-study script](https://github.com/PaulRegular/tinyAM/blob/694039bb4ba31a2419dc587098442ed05ba7af91/analysis/case_study/001_models.R), which uses 1983–2025 and ages 2–14+. Compare fixed natural mortality of 0.3 per year with deviations around `log(0.3)` that are correlated across years and age blocks. Retain the same data, recruitment, cohort survival, fishing mortality and observation specifications. Show the mortality settings and how they enter cohort survival. Use the existing SCAA-, SAM- and NCAM-like fits in the supplement to show how several components can vary together.

```r
m_varying <- ncam
m_constant <- update(ncam, M_settings = list(process = "off"))
```

**Evaluate the hypothesis.** Use `plot_model()` to verify the change in specification and `check_tam()` to assess numerical fit and uncertainty. Inspect age-by-year survey residuals for runs of over- or underprediction. Compare one-year-ahead survey log-RMSE and MASE on identical forecast origins and survey–age observations. Both hindcasts condition on observed aggregate catch. Report the full fold coverage and failures before interpreting score differences.

**Interpret the consequences.** Compare estimated mortality and SSB with uncertainty, and use retrospective peels to assess how terminal estimates change as observations are removed. Examine whether the mortality process is weakly estimated or near a correlation boundary. Interpret any predictive improvement relative to the chosen constant mortality baseline. Discuss what external information on survival, fishing mortality or availability would help distinguish explanations.
